title: Robot Room Cleaner
statement:
A cleaning robot stands in a room that your code cannot see. The room is a grid `room` of `m` rows and `n` columns in which `1` marks an open cell and `0` marks a wall; everything beyond the grid's border is wall as well. The robot starts on the open cell at row `row`, column `col`, facing up (towards row 0). Get the robot to clean every open cell, steering it only through this API:

- `robot.move()`: if the cell in front of the robot is open, the robot steps into it and the call returns `true`; if it is a wall, the robot stays where it is and the call returns `false`.
- `robot.turnLeft()` / `robot.turnRight()`: rotate the robot 90 degrees in place.
- `robot.clean()`: clean the cell the robot is standing on.

Every open cell can be reached from the start. Your function is called as `cleanRoom(robot)`: each case lists `[room, row, col]` only so the judge can build the robot, and none of it is passed to you, so the robot is your first parameter and the others are `undefined`. The answer to a case is the room as it looks when your function returns, with every cell the robot cleaned shown as `2`; a complete clean turns every `1` into a `2` (LeetCode reports this as "Robot cleaned all rooms."). The judge stops a robot that makes more than `200 × (open cells) + 1000` API calls.
constraints: Every open cell can be reached from (row, col)
Local cases have at most 1,500 open cells, so a recursive search stays within the judge's stack
signature: void cleanRoom(int[][] room, int row, int col)
notes:
## Intuition

The robot has no map and no coordinates, so we invent our own: call the start cell `(0, 0)` and track every move relative to it. With that, cleaning is a depth-first search over the open cells, the same flood fill you would run on a visible grid. The twist is that the robot is physically in only one place, so after exploring a branch it has to walk back to where the branch began, facing the way it did before: that undo step is what makes this backtracking. Wandering randomly might also clean everything eventually, but nothing tells it when to stop.

## Approach

1. Number the headings clockwise (`0` up, `1` right, `2` down, `3` left) so that one `turnRight()` adds 1 to the heading; `directions[dir]` is the row and column step for heading `dir`.
2. `backtrack(row, col, facing)` marks the cell in `visited` and cleans it.
3. It then tries the four headings in turn: `dir = (facing + turn) % 4`, the way the robot faces at that moment.
4. If the neighbour in that heading is not visited and `robot.move()` succeeds, recurse into it, then call `goBack()`: turn around, step back, turn around again, which restores both the cell and the heading.
5. Turn right to face the next heading. After four turns the robot faces where it started, so the caller's bookkeeping still holds.
6. Start with `backtrack(0, 0, 0)`, since the robot begins facing up.

## Example 1, step by step

The robot starts at grid cell (1, 3), which it calls `(0, 0)`, facing up. It cleans it, moves up into (0, 3) (its `(-1, 0)`) and cleans that. There, up is the outer wall, so `move()` fails and it turns right; (0, 4) is open, so it moves and recurses with `facing = 1`. From (0, 4) the cell to the right is the wall at (0, 5), so it turns right again and goes down to (1, 4), and so on. Each dead end sends it back with `goBack()` one cell at a time until a cell with an untried heading is found. When the first call finishes, all 30 open cells have been cleaned, so every `1` of the room has become a `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(N): each of the N open cells is entered once and makes at most 4 move attempts plus a constant number of turns (walls cost one failed `move()` each).
- Space: O(N): `visited` holds every open cell, and the recursion can be N levels deep along a long corridor.

## Pitfalls

- The robot's heading must be tracked with the coordinates: after `turnRight()` the next heading is `dir + 1`, so the order of `directions` must be clockwise.
- `goBack()` must end with a second half-turn; stepping back while still facing the wrong way breaks every later direction.
- Check `visited` before calling `move()`, or the robot steps into a cleaned cell and you must walk it back for nothing.
- Each `backtrack` call must make all four right turns, even after recursing, so the robot leaves the cell facing the way it arrived.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `directions` | row and column step for headings up, right, down, left |
| `visited` | cells already cleaned, as `"row,col"` relative to the start |
| `row`, `col` | the robot's current cell relative to the start |
| `facing` | the heading the robot had when it entered this cell |
| `turn`, `dir` | how many right turns were made here, and the heading now faced |
| `nextRow`, `nextCol` | the cell in front of the robot |
